newsitem.title: USA: Senators launch campaign finance reform push.
newsitem.headline: Senators launch campaign finance reform push.

text.p: Two senators on Wednesday launched a new bipartisan push to reform the campaign finance system, hoping to capitalise on growing public disquiet over a scandal involving Democratic fundraising from Asian interests.

Republican Sen. John McCain of Arizona and Wisconsin Democrat Russ Feingold said at a National Press Club luncheon they would formally reintroduce legislation later this month to drastically limit the amount of money being spent on political campaigns.
In the last Senate, a bill they sponsered garnered 55 Senate votes but fell short of the 60 necessary to overcome a filibuster by opponents.

"Politics is timing. If we're going to have reform it has to be this year as a result of the scandals which have motivated the American people to pay attention to this issue," McCain told Reuters in an interview.

The issue came to the forefront in the final weeks of last year's presidential campaign with disclosures that the Democratic Party raised large sums of money from wealthy Asian businessmen, and individuals who could not substantiate the true source of the money they provided.

The Democrats have returned over $1.5 million and face a Justice Department probe and the prospect of congressional hearings. President Bill Clinton is also under the microscope amid allegations that overseas interests donated huge sums of money to influence U.S. foreign policy.
Clinton has said he supports the McCain-Feingold effort but the bill faces powerful opponents inside and outside Congress, who have defeated many previous attempts to pass campaign finance reform.
The current campaign finance legislation was passed in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal in the 1970s. It was designed to limit campaign contributions by individuals to political campaigns.

However most experts say that system is now in ruins. Companies, labour unions and wealthy people have effectively bipassed the limits by contributing large amounts of money directly to the Democratic and Republican parties rather than to individual candidate, or simply by launching their own "issue advocacy" campaigns.
Feingold saids the system was "out of control" and called it a "legalized system of, in effect, bribery."
"What we need is moderate, mutual disarmament in the campaign finance area," he said.
McCain predicted that hearings would uncover more scandalous behaviour, by Republicans as well as Democrats, that would intensify public pressure for reform.
He said the current system led to public cynicism about politics and deterred talented people from entering politics while vastly favouring incumbents.
"With sufficient outside pressure and with sufficient media attention, we can succeed," he said.
